'''James Alan Shapiro''' (born May 18, 1943) is an [[Americans|American]] biologist, an expert in [[bacterial genetics]] and a professor emeritus in the Department of [[Biochemistry]] and [[Molecular Biology]] at the [[University of Chicago]].<ref>{{citation | url=http://bmb.uchospitals.edu/Faculty_and_Research/01_Faculty/01_Faculty_Alphabetically.php?faculty_id=152 | title=Faculty profile |publisher=Department of Biochemistry and Molecular Biology, University of Chicago | access-date=September 20, 2013 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130921055222/http://bmb.uchospitals.edu/Faculty_and_Research/01_Faculty/01_Faculty_Alphabetically.php?faculty_id=152 | archive-date=September 21, 2013 | url-status=dead }}</ref>

==Academic biography==
Shapiro obtained his bachelor's degree in English from [[Harvard College]] in 1964.<ref name="crimson"/><ref name="bwsp">{{citation|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1992/10/13/science/the-biologist-who-saw-a-pattern.html|title=The Biologist Who Saw a Pattern|first=Gina|last=Kolata|authorlink=Gina Kolata|journal=[[New York Times]]|date=October 13, 1992}}</ref> Then, inspired by a [[genetics]] course he had taken as a senior,<ref name="beckwith">{{citation|title=Making genes, making waves: a social activist in science|first=Jonathan R.|last=Beckwith|publisher=Harvard University Press|year=2002|isbn=978-0-674-00928-8|url-access=registration|url=https://archive.org/details/makinggenesmakin0000beck}}</ref> he shifted from English to science. He was awarded a [[Marshall Scholarship]] for postgraduate research at [[Corpus Christi College, Cambridge]], from 1964 to 1967, spending his final year at [[Hammersmith]] hospital under the supervision of [[William Hayes (geneticist)|William Hayes]], and being awarded a PhD in genetics in 1968.
His thesis, ''The Structure of the Galactose Operon in Escherichia coli K12'', contains the first suggestion of [[Transposable element|transposable elements]] in bacteria. He confirmed this hypothesis in 1968 during his postdoctoral tenure as a Jane Coffin Childs fellow in the laboratory of François Jacob at the Institut Pasteur in Paris.

As an American Cancer Society fellow in [[Jon Beckwith]]’s laboratory at the [[Harvard Medical School]] 1968-70, he and his colleagues used in vivo genetic manipulations to clone and purify the lac operon of E. coli.

He was troubled by the potential [[genetic engineering]] applications of his research.<ref name="beckwith"/><ref>{{citation|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1996/03/05/science/elusive-genetic-switch-at-last-yields-image-of-its-3-d-structure.html|title=Elusive Genetic Switch At Last Yields Image Of Its 3-D Structure|first=Gina|last=Kolata|authorlink=Gina Kolata|journal=[[New York Times]]|date=March 5, 1996}}</ref><ref>{{citation|title=Harvard Geneticist Turns to Social Ills|journal=[[Boston Globe]]|first=Richard|last=Knox|date=January 20, 1970}}</ref>

He served as Invited Professor in the School of Biological Sciences at the University of Havana, Cuba 1970-1972, before returning to another postdoctorate with [[Harlyn O. Halvorson|Harlyn Halvorson]] at [[Brandeis University]].<ref name="bwsp"/> Since 1973, he has worked as a professor of microbiology at the University of Chicago.

In 1975 Shapiro attended the ICN-[[UCLA]] [[Squaw Valley, Placer County, California|Squaw Valley]] Symposium on Bacterial [[Plasmid]]s, where his interest in [[DNA]] restructuring in bacteria was heightened by learning about the movements of antibiotic resistance transposons to new genomic locations. This prompted him to organize, in collaboration with [[Sankar Adhya]] and the late Ahmed Bukhari, the first meeting on the topic of DNA insertion elements at [[Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory]] in 1976. Although they expected only a few colleagues, the meeting was attended by over 150 scientists from around the world, including [[Barbara McClintock]]. McClintock had first identified [[transposition (horizontal gene transfer)]] (movement to new genomic location) of DNA "controlling elements" in maize (sweetcorn) in 1948, for which discovery she was awarded a Nobel Prize 1983. Shapiro and McClintock continued their collaboration up until her death in 1992.<ref>{{Cite web| title=Perspectives - Letting Escherichia coli Teach Me About Genome Engineering | author=James A. Shapiro | url=https://shapiro.bsd.uchicago.edu/Shapiro.2009.GeneticsPerspective.pdf | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100612231840/http://shapiro.bsd.uchicago.edu/Shapiro.2009.GeneticsPerspective.pdf | archive-date=2010-06-12}}</ref>

He has also been a visiting professor from time to time, including once as a Darwin Prize Visiting Professor at the [[University of Edinburgh]] in 1994.<ref>{{citation  | url = http://shapiro.bsd.uchicago.edu/cv.shtml | title=Curriculum Vitae, James A. Shapiro | publisher=University of Chicago}}</ref>

==Research==
While working with Beckwith at Harvard, Shapiro was lead author of the first team to isolate a single [[gene]] from an organism.<ref name="bwsp"/><ref>{{citation|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1969/11/23/archives/scientists-isolate-a-gene-step-in-heredity-control-scientists.html|title=Scientists Isolate a Gene; Step in Heredity Control|journal=[[New York Times]]|date=November 23, 1969}}</ref><ref>{{citation|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1969/12/08/archives/playing-with-biological-fire.html|title=Playing With Biological Fire|journal=[[New York Times]]|date=December 8, 1969}}</ref> The gene they isolated was ''[[lac operon|lacZ]]'', which codes for the [[β-galactosidase]] [[enzyme]] used by ''[[E. coli]]'' bacteria to digest the sugars in milk. Their technique involved [[Transduction (genetics)|transduction]] to clone oppositely oriented copies of the gene inserted into two specialized transducing bacteriophages, then mixing single-stranded DNA from the two phages so that only the bacterial sequences would form a double helix, and finally using a [[nuclease]] to degrade the single-stranded phage sequences, leaving only the double-stranded ''lacZ'' DNA.<ref>{{citation|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=ppRmC9-a6JQC&pg=PA42|title=The lac Operon: a short history of a genetic paradigm|first=Benno|last=Müller-Hill|publisher=Walter de Gruyter|year=1996|isbn=978-3-11-014830-5|page=42}}</ref>

In a paper published in the ''[[Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America|Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences]]'' in 1979, Shapiro was the first to propose [[replicative transposition]] as a detailed molecular mechanism for genetic mobility by transposable elements, such as the Tn3 ampicillin resistance transposon and transposing bacteriophage Mu. In this model, the ends of transposable elements covalently bond to target site DNA sequences via a process that forms an intermediate structure with replication forks at each end of the transposing element, sometimes called a "Shapiro intermediate".<ref>{{citation|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=8oIaOGHURroC&pg=PA46|title=Lateral DNA transfer: mechanisms and consequences|first=Frederic|last=Bushman|publisher=CSHL Press|year=2002|isbn=978-0-87969-621-4|page=46}}</ref>

In other research, Shapiro showed that bacteria organize themselves spatially as they grow in communities on agar surfaces. For instance, he analyzed how each strain of the sometimes pathogenic bacterium ''[[Proteus mirabilis]]'' forms its own pattern of complex terraced rings by periodic group “swarm" migration, an emergent property that can be explained by mathematical rules derived by a physicist collaborator, Sergei Esipov. Shapiro related this to other complex multicellular behaviors, such as hunting, building protective structures, spreading spores, and individual bacteria sacrificing themselves for the benefit of the larger community.<ref>{{citation|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1988/07/05/science/some-thoughts-on-self-sacrifice.html|title=Some Thoughts on Self Sacrifice|first=Malcolm W.|last=Browne|journal=[[New York Times]]|date=July 5, 1988}}</ref><ref>{{citation|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1992/10/13/science/bacteria-are-found-to-thrive-on-a-rich-social-life.html|title=Bacteria Are Found to Thrive on a Rich Social Life|journal=[[New York Times]]|first=Gina|last=Kolata|authorlink=Gina Kolata|date=October 13, 1992}}</ref><ref>{{citation|title=Scientist uncovers secret lives of bacteria|journal=[[Chicago Sun-Times]]|date=December 15, 2004|first=Sandra|last=Guy}}</ref> Based on this work, Shapiro believes that cooperative behavior is a fundamental organizing concept for biological activity at all levels of complexity.<ref>{{citation|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1992/04/14/science/biologists-tally-generosity-s-rewards.html|title=Biologists Tally Generosity's Rewards|journal=[[New York Times]]|first=Malcolm W.|last=Browne|date=April 14, 1992}}</ref>

==Natural genetic engineering==
He has proposed the term [[natural genetic engineering]] to account for how novelty is created in the course of biological evolution. It has been criticized by some,<ref>{{citation |last=Bezak |first=Eva |year=2011 |title=(Review) Evolution: A View from the 21st Century |journal=Australasian Physical & Engineering Science in Medicine |volume=34 |issue=4 |pages=643–645|doi=10.1007/s13246-011-0110-4 }}</ref><ref>{{citation |last=Buratti |first=Emanuele |year=2012 |title=(Review) Evolutionary Lessons for 21st Century Molecular Biotechnologists |journal=Molecular Biotechnology |volume=52 |issue=1 |pages=89–90|doi=10.1007/s12033-011-9472-9 }}</ref><ref>{{citation |last=Moran |first=Laurence A |date=May–June 2011 |title=(Review) Evolution: A View from the 21st Century |journal=Reports of the National Center for Science Education |volume=32 |issue=3 |pages=10 |url=https://ncse.ngo/sites/default/files/pdfs/32_3_P_final.pdf}}</ref><ref>{{citation |last=Seoighe |first=Cathal |year=2012 |title=(Review) Evolution: A View from the 21st Century |journal=Trends in Evolutionary Biology |volume=4 |issue=e6 |pages=32–33|doi=10.4081/eb.2012.e6 |doi-access=free }}</ref> and Shapiro has responded to points raised by his critics.<ref name="Shapiro 2012">{{citation | title=Response to Pauline Hogeweg's review of my book, "Evolution: a view from the 21st century" | author=Shapiro, James A. | journal=Evolutionary Intelligence | year=2012 | doi=10.1007/s12065-012-0074-7 | volume=5 | issue=3 | page=211| doi-access=free }}</ref>

Shapiro maintains that many genome changes that occur naturally operate by similar molecular DNA rearrangements to those applied intentionally by scientists using genetic engineering techniques developed over the last few decades. For example, transposable elements may be amplified and moved to different locations in the genome. These DNA changes have been found to result in distributed genomic networks for the execution of a wide range of complex traits in fungi, diatoms, plants and animals, such as flower development, the vertebrate body plan, viviparous reproduction and nervous system development in various mammals.<ref>{{citation|url=https://shapiro.bsd.uchicago.edu/Distributed_genome_network_innovation_attributed_to_mobile_DNA_elements.html|title = Distributed genome network innovation attributed to mobile DNA elements}}</ref>

==The Third Way of Evolution==

Shapiro and [[Denis Noble]] established [[The Third Way of Evolution]] (TWE) project in 2014. The TWE which is also known as the "Integrated Synthesis" shares many similarities with the [[extended evolutionary synthesis]] but is more extreme in its claims.<ref name="Svensson 2023">{{citation | chapter-url=https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-031-22028-9_11 | doi=10.1007/978-3-031-22028-9_11 | chapter=The Structure of Evolutionary Theory: Beyond Neo-Darwinism, Neo-Lamarckism and Biased Historical Narratives About the Modern Synthesis |editor1=Dickins, T.E. |editor2=Dickins, B.J.| title=Evolutionary Biology: Contemporary and Historical Reflections Upon Core Theory | series=Evolutionary Biology – New Perspectives on Its Development | date=2023 | last1=Svensson | first1=Erik I. | volume=6 | pages=173–217 | isbn=978-3-031-22027-2 }}</ref> The TWE consists of a group of researchers who provide a middle path "Third Way" alternative to [[creationism]] and the [[Modern synthesis (20th century)|modern synthesis]]. The TWE predicts that the modern synthesis will be replaced with an entirely new evolutionary framework.<ref name="Svensson 2023"/> As of 2023 only a very small minority of evolutionary biologists currently support the TWE and it has been described as a "[[fringe movement]]".<ref name="Svensson 2023"/>

==Awards and honors==
Shapiro was elected to [[Phi Beta Kappa]] in 1963<ref>{{citation|title=16 Elected Phi Beta Kappa At Harvard|journal=[[Boston Globe]]|date=December 8, 1963}}</ref> and was a [[Marshall Scholar]] from 1964 to 1966.<ref name="crimson"/> He won the Darwin Prize Visiting Professorship of the [[University of Edinburgh]] in 1993.<ref name="ucc-obe"/> In 1994, he was elected as a [[fellow]] of the [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]] for "innovative and creative interpretations of bacterial genetics and growth, especially the action of mobile genetic elements and the formation of bacterial colonies."<ref name="AAAS Fellow listing"/><ref>{{citation|url=http://chronicle.uchicago.edu/950119/aaas.shtml|journal=University of Chicago Chronicle|title=Four faculty members elected AAAS Fellows|date=January 19, 1995|volume=14|issue=10}}</ref> And in 2001, he was made an honorary officer of the [[Order of the British Empire]] for his service to the Marshall Scholarship program.<ref name="ucc-obe"/> In 2014 he was chosen to give the 3rd annual "Nobel Prize Laureate - Robert G. Edwards" lecture <ref>{{Cite web|url=https://cogi-congress.org/|title=World Congress Controversies in Obstetrics, Gynecology and Infertility.}}</ref>

==Selected publications==
Shapiro edited the books ''Mobile Genetic Elements'' (Academic Press, 1983) and, with Martin Dworkin, ''Bacteria as Multicellular Organisms'' (Oxford University Press, 1997). He is the author of ''Evolution: A View from the 21st Century'' (FT Press Science, 2011, {{ISBN|978-0-13-278093-3}}).

In 2022 Shapiro published a greatly expanded and updated second edition of ''Evolution: A View from the 21st Century'' (Cognition Press, {{ISBN|978-1-7374987-0-4}}).

Shapiro, [[Denis Noble]], [[Peter A. Corning]], [[Addy Pross]] and [[Stuart A. Kauffman]] authored 2023's ''Evolution "On Purpose": Teleonomy in Living Systems''.<ref>[https://mitpress.mit.edu/9780262546409/evolution-on-purpose/ ''Evolution "On Purpose": Teleonomy in Living Systems''] (2023) mitpress.mit.edu.</ref>
